name: Thomas Heatherwick
bio: Heatherwick is not a licensed architect, a fact his admirers cite as liberation and his critics as diagnosis. Trained in three-dimensional design at Manchester Polytechnic and the Royal College of Art, and championed early by Terence Conran, he founded his London studio in 1994 and set it to work on buses, bridges, handbags and buildings as if they were the same problem of making. The Seed Cathedral at the 2010 Shanghai Expo made his name; a run of New York commissions — Vessel, Little Island — made him the developer's favorite spectacle-builder. The misses are as public as the hits: the Garden Bridge consumed some 43 million pounds of mostly public money without breaking ground, and Vessel closed repeatedly after suicides before reopening with nets. Since 2023 he has campaigned against 'boring' buildings under the banner of his book Humanise; whatever else is said of his own, nobody has called them that.

projects.title: Seed Cathedral (UK Pavilion, Expo 2010)
projects.blurb: A box bristling with 60,000 transparent acrylic rods, each tipped with real seeds from Kew's seed bank; it won the Expo's top pavilion prize and made the studio's name.

projects.title: Vessel
projects.blurb: A 46-meter climbable lattice of 154 interlocking stairs at Hudson Yards — a landmark with no program, closed and re-engineered after a series of suicides.

projects.title: Little Island
projects.blurb: A park and amphitheater carried above the Hudson on 132 concrete 'tulip' piles, paid for almost entirely by Barry Diller.

projects.title: Zeitz MOCAA
projects.blurb: A 1920s grain silo carved open into a cathedral-like atrium for Africa's largest contemporary art museum.
projects.wikipedia: Zeitz Museum of Contemporary Art Africa

projects.title: Coal Drops Yard
projects.blurb: Two Victorian coal warehouses at King's Cross joined by roofs that swoop up to kiss — industrial heritage remade as retail theater.

projects.title: Learning Hub
projects.blurb: Twelve towers of cornerless, concrete tutorial rooms stacked like dim-sum baskets for Nanyang Technological University.

projects.title: Azabudai Hills
projects.blurb: An undulating, garden-covered low-rise landscape threading between Pelli Clarke's towers in central Tokyo.

projects.title: Google Bay View
projects.blurb: With BIG: tent-like canopies clad in 'dragonscale' solar tiles over two vast open workfloors.

projects.title: New Routemaster
projects.blurb: The double-decker bus reimagined with a wraparound glass stair and open rear platform — public transport as civic design.

projects.title: Rolling Bridge
projects.blurb: A Paddington footbridge that curls into an octagon like a caterpillar rather than lifting — the early work that fixed his reputation for mechanical wit.

name: Sou Fujimoto
bio: Fujimoto grew up in rural Hokkaido, the son of a psychiatrist, and has spent his career asking where the forest ends and the building begins. After Tokyo University and several unbuilt years, he founded his office in 2000 and worked out his ideas at domestic scale: houses like House N and House NA that dissolve walls, floors and privacy into nested shells and tree-branch platforms, under a theory he called 'primitive future.' The 2013 Serpentine Pavilion — a white steel cloud you could climb — made him, at 41, the youngest architect then given the commission. The second act went big and went abroad: a balcony-feathered tower in Montpellier, a perforated concert hall in Budapest, and the master planning of Expo 2025 Osaka, where his two-kilometer Grand Ring became the largest wooden structure ever built. Few architects have scaled from 60-square-meter houses to national spectacle with the ideas so intact.

projects.title: Grand Ring
projects.blurb: The two-kilometer timber ring encircling Expo 2025 — traditional joinery at infrastructural scale, certified the largest wooden structure in the world.

projects.title: Serpentine Gallery Pavilion 2013
projects.blurb: A climbable cloud of white 20mm steel lattice, blurring architecture into landscape on the Serpentine lawn.

projects.title: House NA
projects.blurb: A fully transparent house of 21 staggered floor plates on a Tokyo street — living in a tree, with the neighbors watching.

projects.title: House N
projects.blurb: Three nested, perforated white shells grading from street to bedroom; his clearest statement that a house is a gradient, not a boundary.

projects.title: Musashino Art University Museum & Library
projects.blurb: A library made of a single spiraling wall of bookshelves — the shelf as structure, plan and idea at once.

projects.title: L'Arbre Blanc
projects.blurb: A residential tower feathered with 194 cantilevered balconies, designed to be lived on rather than in.

projects.title: House of Music Hungary
projects.blurb: A concert hall under a perforated canopy pierced by the trees of Budapest's City Park.

projects.title: Final Wooden House
projects.blurb: A bungalow stacked from massive 350mm cedar beams that serve as floor, seat, wall and stair interchangeably.

projects.title: Shiroiya Hotel
projects.blurb: A 1970s hotel gutted to a four-story concrete atrium and joined by a grassy hill of new rooms — the anchor of Maebashi's regeneration.

projects.title: Children's Psychiatric Rehabilitation Center
projects.blurb: White boxes scattered like dice to make in-between spaces where troubled children can hide without being lost; the early work where his ideas first turned social.

name: Tatiana Bilbao
bio: Bilbao's grandfather Tomás was a Basque architect who fled Franco's Spain for Mexico City, where she was born in 1972 into a family that argued about buildings at dinner. After the Universidad Iberoamericana she spent two years inside the city's urban housing ministry, an education in how most Mexicans actually live that never left her work. She opened her estudio in 2004, banned photorealistic renderings in favor of collage, and built a practice that swings from a house designed with Gabriel Orozco to an 8,000-dollar expandable dwelling shown at the 2015 Chicago Biennial. The botanical garden in Culiacán, accreted patiently over two decades with commissioned artworks, is the office's method in miniature: slow, collaborative, unfinished on principle. She teaches at Yale and argues, persistently, that housing is a right rather than a commodity.

projects.title: Jardín Botánico de Culiacán
projects.blurb: A two-decade masterplan threading concrete pavilions and commissioned artworks — Turrell included — through an existing botanical garden; a project designed never to be finished.

projects.title: Gran Acuario Mazatlán
projects.blurb: An aquarium of the Sea of Cortez built as a grid of monumental raw-concrete halls, like a ruin flooded on purpose.

projects.title: Sustainable Housing Prototype
projects.blurb: An 8,000-dollar expandable house — concrete core, wooden-pallet wings — designed for Mexico's housing deficit and first shown at the Chicago Architecture Biennial.

projects.title: Casa Ventura
projects.blurb: Pentagonal concrete modules cascading down a wooded slope of the Sierra Madre, a house arranged like a small village.

projects.title: Los Terrenos
projects.blurb: A weekend house split into mirrored-glass, clay-brick and rammed-earth volumes that let the forest do the composing.

projects.title: Observatory House
projects.blurb: A house conceived with artist Gabriel Orozco after the Jantar Mantar observatory in Jaipur — a bathing pool at the center of a concrete instrument for watching the sky.

projects.title: Ruta del Peregrino Lookout Point
projects.blurb: A spiraling concrete gazebo on a pilgrimage route walked by two million people a year — infrastructure for rest and vertigo.

projects.title: Bioinnova
projects.blurb: A stacked, cantilevered research and teaching building for Tec de Monterrey, its floors shifted to make shaded terraces.

projects.title: Casa Ajijic
projects.blurb: A house of rammed earth on Lake Chapala, arguing that the cheapest local material could carry contemporary form.

projects.title: Tangassi Funeral Home
projects.blurb: An early commission that treated grief architecturally — quiet courtyards and filtered light instead of the industry's marble kitsch.

name: Bjarke Ingels
bio: Ingels enrolled in architecture school in Copenhagen hoping it would make him a better cartoonist, and in a sense it did: his 2009 manifesto Yes Is More was published as a comic book. After Barcelona and a formative stint at OMA under Koolhaas, he co-founded PLOT in 2001 and then BIG in 2005, preaching 'hedonistic sustainability' — the idea that the responsible building should also be the most fun. Copenhagen got the proofs: a housing block you cycle up, a harbor you swim in, a power plant you ski down. He moved to New York in 2012 and scaled the act globally, from a court-scraper on the Hudson to Google campuses, with side quests into floating cities and Mars simulations. Critics call it architainment; an unusual number of people live, work and ski happily inside the argument.

projects.title: CopenHill
projects.blurb: A waste-to-energy plant with a ski slope on its roof and a climbing wall up its chimney facade — hedonistic sustainability stated as bluntly as possible.

projects.title: 8 House
projects.blurb: A figure-eight block of 475 homes in Ørestad with a public path cycling from street level to the tenth floor.

projects.title: Mountain Dwellings
projects.blurb: Eighty terraced apartments draped over a parking garage — suburban garden life stacked at urban density.

projects.title: VM Houses
projects.blurb: With PLOT partner Julien De Smedt: two slabs bent into a V and an M, bristling with pointed balconies to steal light and views.

projects.title: VIA 57 West
projects.blurb: The 'courtscraper' — a Copenhagen courtyard block stretched into a 142-meter hyperbolic pyramid on the West Side Highway.

projects.title: Maritime Museum of Denmark
projects.blurb: A museum wrapped invisibly around a dry dock beside Hamlet's castle, its galleries below grade and its void the exhibit.

projects.title: LEGO House
projects.blurb: Twenty-one stacked volumes in brick proportion for the brick's hometown, crowned by a 2x4 keystone.

projects.title: Superkilen
projects.blurb: With Superflex and Topotek 1: a kilometer-long park in Nørrebro furnished with objects from the 60-odd home countries of its neighbors.

projects.title: The Twist
projects.blurb: A gallery that bridges the Randselva river with a 90-degree torque midspan, doubling as the entrance sequence of the Kistefos sculpture park.

projects.title: Copenhagen Harbour Bath
projects.blurb: With PLOT: a public swimming pool cut into the cleaned-up harbor at Islands Brygge — the small project that announced the whole civic program.

name: Junya Ishigami
bio: Ishigami spent four years at SANAA before founding his own office in 2004, and then set about out-thinning his teachers. Working with engineer Jun Sato, he pushes structure to the edge of disappearance: the KAIT workshop scatters 305 white columns, some bearing millimeters from buckling, until a room reads as a birch grove. He won the Golden Lion at Venice in 2010 for an installation of carbon-fiber filaments so slight a cat could have destroyed it — one nearly did. His mature work trades speed for geology: a water garden in Nasu made by transplanting 318 trees among 160 hand-dug ponds, a restaurant in Ube cast by pouring concrete into holes excavated in raw earth. The 2019 Serpentine commission brought a rebuke over unpaid internships at his office, a reminder that weightlessness is labor-intensive. Nobody working today makes buildings that look less built.

projects.title: KAIT Workshop
projects.blurb: A single glass room for the Kanagawa Institute of Technology held up by 305 slender white steel columns, no two alike — a structural forest students wander rather than occupy.

projects.title: KAIT Plaza
projects.blurb: A companion hall roofed by a 12-millimeter steel plate sagging naturally over a 90-meter span, its floor curving with it — furniture-less, program-less, and startling.

projects.title: Serpentine Pavilion 2019
projects.blurb: A hill of 61 tons of Cumbrian slate hovering on a grid of thin columns — a stone cloud grown from the lawn.

projects.title: Art Biotop Water Garden
projects.blurb: 318 trees moved one by one from an adjacent site and replanted among 160 shallow ponds; landscape design that won the inaugural Obel Award as architecture.

projects.title: House & Restaurant
projects.blurb: Concrete poured into holes dug in the ground, then excavated — a chef's home and restaurant with the light and gravity of a found cave.

projects.title: Zaishui Art Museum
projects.blurb: A kilometer-long museum skimming a man-made lake, its roof a single line and the water lapping directly against its galleries.

projects.title: Chapel of Valley
projects.blurb: A wedge of chapel 45 meters tall and barely over a meter wide at its narrowest — devotion expressed as a sliver of light.

projects.title: Japan Pavilion, Venice Biennale
projects.blurb: Delicate greenhouses furnished like rooms around Takamasa Yoshizaka's pavilion, dissolving the boundary between exhibition, garden and building.

projects.title: House with Plants
projects.blurb: A small house whose ground floor is a planted garden with a soil floor, the family living above and among it.

projects.title: Balloon
projects.blurb: A one-ton, four-story aluminum balloon floating on helium in the atrium of the Museum of Contemporary Art Tokyo — a building's worth of mass made weightless.

name: Ma Yansong
bio: Ma grew up in Beijing's hutongs, studied at Yale, passed briefly through Zaha Hadid's office, and founded MAD in 2004 with a theory he calls the Shanshui City — high-density urbanism modeled on the mountains and water of classical Chinese landscape painting rather than the Manhattan grid. In 2006 he won the competition for the Absolute Towers in suburban Toronto, the first major overseas landmark by a China-based architect; locals immediately nicknamed the curving pair 'Marilyn Monroe,' which did the marketing for him. Harbin Opera House wrapped that sensibility in aluminum and snow, while his Hutong Bubbles grafted mirrored bathrooms onto aging courtyard houses back home. Two decades on, the practice spans Rome, Paris and Los Angeles, where the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art — a hovering white form seven years in construction — opens in September 2026. His buildings look computational but begin as ink sketches; the softness is the point.

projects.title: Harbin Opera House
projects.blurb: Sinuous aluminum-clad dunes rising from the Songhua River wetlands, with a public path over the roof and an ash-lined hall inside — MAD's fullest built statement.

projects.title: Absolute World
projects.blurb: Twin towers rotating up to eight degrees per floor; the competition win at age 30 that made a Chinese firm a global one.

projects.title: Lucas Museum of Narrative Art
projects.blurb: George Lucas's billion-dollar museum in Exposition Park, a hovering biomorphic shell over 100,000 square feet of galleries, opening September 2026.

projects.title: Ordos Museum
projects.blurb: A bronze-scaled dune of a museum built for a new city that barely arrived — civic optimism landed in the Gobi.

projects.title: Chaoyang Park Plaza
projects.blurb: Black glass towers rising from Beijing's largest park like ink-wash mountains — the Shanshui City argued at skyline scale, to loud disagreement.

projects.title: Hutong Bubble 32
projects.blurb: A mirrored blob containing a bathroom and stair grafted onto a decaying courtyard house — acupuncture, not demolition, for the old city.

projects.title: Jiaxing Train Station
projects.blurb: The 'station in a forest': main functions sunk below grade, a rebuilt 1907 station house above, and 1,500 trees where the usual plaza of paving would be.

projects.title: Quzhou Stadium
projects.blurb: A 30,000-seat stadium buried in an artificial landform, its rim rising like a crater — sport hidden inside landscape.

projects.title: Cloudscape of Haikou
projects.blurb: A seafront library and pavilion of continuous white concrete voids, poured almost without straight lines.

projects.title: Fake Hills
projects.blurb: A kilometer of housing whose roofline undulates like a mountain ridge, with gardens along the crest — the housing block as landscape painting.

name: Frida Escobedo
bio: Escobedo studied at the Universidad Iberoamericana and Harvard's GSD, and built her early reputation on temporary work — pavilions and installations that treated time, not concrete, as the primary material. La Tallera in Cuernavaca announced her in 2012: she rotated two giant Siqueiros murals to open the muralist's studio to the street, a renovation that behaved like a manifesto. In 2018 she became the youngest architect then to build the Serpentine Pavilion, a courtyard of stacked British roof tiles aligned to the Greenwich meridian. Four years later the Metropolitan Museum chose her over a shortlist of established firms to design its 550-million-dollar Tang Wing for modern art — the first woman to design a wing in the Met's history — with construction begun in 2026 toward a 2030 opening. Her signature is the celosía, the perforated screen that filters light, air and visibility; her buildings withhold as much as they show.

projects.title: Tang Wing, Metropolitan Museum of Art
projects.blurb: The Met's new 126,000-square-foot wing for modern and contemporary art, wrapped in a limestone celosía — the first wing in the museum's history designed by a woman, opening 2030.

projects.title: Serpentine Pavilion 2018
projects.blurb: A courtyard enclosed by lattice walls of stacked British roof tiles, with a mirrored canopy and a shallow pool aligned to the prime meridian.

projects.title: La Tallera
projects.blurb: Siqueiros's studio turned public museum by rotating two monumental murals to face a new plaza behind a concrete-block screen — her breakthrough.

projects.title: El Eco Pavilion
projects.blurb: A temporary courtyard of gray concrete blocks at Mathias Goeritz's experimental museum, rearranged by visitors over the summer.

projects.title: Hotel Boca Chica
projects.blurb: A faded 1950s Acapulco hotel restored to tropical-modern economy with José Rojas — the commission that launched her independent practice.

projects.title: Civic Stage
projects.blurb: A tilting, rotating public platform for the Lisbon Architecture Triennale — a stage that made assembly itself the architecture.

projects.title: You Know You Cannot See Yourself So Well as by Reflection
projects.blurb: A field of mirrored-steel screens in the V&A courtyard tracing the meridian, folding London and its colonial timekeeping back on themselves.

projects.title: The Ray Harlem
projects.blurb: A housing tower on 125th Street that rebuilds the National Black Theatre into its base — her first ground-up New York building.

projects.title: Hotel San Cristóbal
projects.blurb: A Baja beach hotel of plain block, color and shadow, resisting the resort industry's usual theming.

projects.title: Aesop Park Slope
projects.blurb: A small Brooklyn store lined in woven brick — the celosía miniaturized into retail, and proof the ideas survive at any scale.

name: Mariam Kamara
bio: Kamara — now practicing as Mariam Issoufou — worked for years as a software engineer in the United States before an architecture master's at the University of Washington redirected her to Niamey, where she founded atelier masōmī in 2014. Her position is blunt: compressed earth, the Sahel's oldest material, is cheaper, cooler and more dignified than the imported concrete that signals progress, and she has the buildings to prove it. In Dandaji she turned a crumbling mosque into a library and built a new raw-earth mosque beside it; in Niamey she housed four families on a plot that convention said fit one. A Rolex mentorship under David Adjaye seeded the Niamey Cultural Center, and commissions followed across the continent — a museum near Senegal's megaliths, Ellen Johnson Sirleaf's presidential center in Monrovia. She holds the chair for Architecture Heritage and Sustainability at ETH Zurich, exporting the argument to the discipline's center from its supposed periphery.

projects.title: Hikma Community Complex
projects.blurb: With Yasaman Esmaili: a derelict adobe mosque restored as a library, sharing its site with a new compressed-earth mosque — secular and sacred knowledge deliberately side by side.

projects.title: Dandaji Regional Market
projects.blurb: Market stalls of compressed earth shaded by recycled-metal canopies on slender columns, reviving a weekly market and the village economy with it.

projects.title: Niamey 2000
projects.blurb: With united4design: four family homes in compressed earth on a single-family plot, a density prototype for a fast-growing capital; shortlisted for the Aga Khan Award.

projects.title: Bët-bi Museum
projects.blurb: A museum and community center rising near the Senegambian stone circles for the Albers Foundation and Le Korsa — contemporary art returned to a sacred landscape.

projects.title: Ellen Johnson Sirleaf Presidential Center
projects.blurb: The world's first presidential library for a female head of state, drawn from Liberia's palava-hut tradition and designed by an all-woman team.

projects.title: Niamey Cultural Center
projects.blurb: A cultural complex of raised earthen towers developed during her Rolex protégé year with David Adjaye — the Sahel's building tradition scaled to civic ambition.

projects.title: Yantala Office
projects.blurb: An office building applying the studio's earthen construction and passive-cooling logic to the commercial workplace.

projects.title: Process
projects.blurb: An installation at the 2023 Venice Architecture Biennale unpacking how a Niamey mosque is actually made — labor and material as the exhibit.

projects.title: Kollo Elementary School
projects.blurb: Village classrooms built around shade and cross-ventilation — the office's civic playbook at its most everyday.

projects.title: Mobile Loitering
projects.blurb: Her thesis project: mobile canopies claiming public space for Niamey's women and young people, the research seed of everything after.

name: Lina Ghotmeh
bio: Ghotmeh was born in Beirut in 1980, mid-civil-war, and has said she grew up assuming ruins were a natural building type; she calls her method an 'archaeology of the future.' Trained at the American University of Beirut and seasoned at Ateliers Jean Nouvel in Paris, she was in her mid-twenties when she and two colleagues won the Estonian National Museum competition, founding DGT to build it — a kilometer-long museum lifting off a Soviet airbase runway, completed in 2016. Her own Paris office followed, and with it Stone Garden, a hand-troweled Beirut tower that rode out the 2020 port explosion weeks after completion. The commissions since read like a run of institutional trust: low-carbon brick workshops for Hermès, the 2023 Serpentine Pavilion, Bahrain's dhow-inspired pavilion at Expo 2025 Osaka — voted the fair's best — and, in 2025, the redesign of the British Museum's entire Western Range, the largest rebuilding in its history. She builds heavily, deliberately, in an age of renders; the work argues that memory is a construction material.

projects.title: Estonian National Museum
projects.blurb: With DGT: a 355-meter museum rising off the runway of a Soviet airbase, turning an instrument of occupation into a national front door.

projects.title: Stone Garden
projects.blurb: A residential tower coated in hand-combed earthen render, its windows planted with gardens; it withstood the port explosion weeks after completion.

projects.title: Hermès Leather Workshops
projects.blurb: Low, arched workshops of half a million bricks — France's first energy-positive industrial building, made for a company that measures time in decades.

projects.title: Serpentine Pavilion 2023 — À table
projects.blurb: A shallow timber dome sheltering one long communal table, its structure ribbed like a palm leaf — architecture as an invitation to sit down together.

projects.title: Bahrain Pavilion, Expo 2025
projects.blurb: A timber pavilion assembled like a dhow's hull without permanent fixings, awarded gold for best architecture at the Expo.

projects.title: British Museum Western Range
projects.blurb: The competition-winning redesign of a third of the British Museum's galleries — the largest transformation in the institution's 270-year history.

projects.title: Les Grands Verres
projects.blurb: The Palais de Tokyo's restaurant rebuilt around a monumental rammed-earth bar and reclaimed materials — fine dining with a mud manifesto.

projects.title: AlUla Contemporary Art Museum
projects.blurb: A museum woven into the oasis landscape of AlUla, extending her archaeological method to an actual archaeological landscape.

projects.title: Réalimenter Masséna
projects.blurb: A Réinventer Paris competition winner: a timber tower for urban food culture grown around a disused rail station.

projects.title: Light in Water
projects.blurb: With DGT: a centenary installation of falling water droplets frozen by strobing light — architecture reduced to rain and time.

name: Tosin Oshinowo
bio: Oshinowo trained in London, then returned to Lagos and worked as lead architect on liquefied-natural-gas projects at James Cubitt before founding cmDesign Atelier in 2013 — rebranded Oshinowo Studio a decade later. She coined 'Afro-minimalism' for her pared-back houses threaded with Yoruba material culture, and extended the idea into Ilé Ilà, a furniture line upholstered in àdìrẹ and asò-oké. The work runs from beach pavilions on the Ilashe peninsula to Maryland Mall's giant LED facade, but the project that shifted her reputation was Ngarannam: a whole town in Borno State — 564 homes, school, clinic, market — rebuilt with the UNDP for a community displaced by Boko Haram. In 2023 she curated the Sharjah Architecture Triennial under the title The Beauty of Impermanence, an argument that the Global South's adaptive, improvised building cultures are a resource rather than a deficit. A 2025 Loeb Fellowship at Harvard confirmed what Lagos already knew: she is the most visible voice of a new Nigerian architecture.

projects.title: Ngarannam Resettlement Town
projects.blurb: A town rebuilt with the UNDP for a community displaced by Boko Haram — 564 climate-adapted homes plus school, clinic, market and barracks, designed with the returning residents.

projects.title: Coral Pavilion
projects.blurb: An all-white beach house on the Lagos peninsula, reachable only by boat, its colonnade framing the Atlantic — Afro-minimalism at its most distilled.

projects.title: Maryland Mall
projects.blurb: A retail landmark on Ikorodu Road fronted by one of West Africa's largest LED screens; the commercial project that made her name at home.

projects.title: Adidas Flagship Store
projects.blurb: The brand's first West African flagship, a 1970s building retrofitted and wrapped in perforated corrugated aluminium — the material of Lagos mass housing made luxurious.

projects.title: Sharjah Architecture Triennial 2023
projects.blurb: As curator: The Beauty of Impermanence framed the Global South's adaptive reuse and improvised building as design intelligence, not scarcity.

projects.title: Sencillo Beach House
projects.blurb: A three-bedroom weekend house of simple volumes and deep shade on the Ilashe shore, the first of her beach-house series.

projects.title: Fowóralé House
projects.blurb: A beach residence organized around courtyards and cross-ventilation, refining the studio's tropical-minimal vocabulary.

projects.title: Ilé Ilà
projects.blurb: 'House of Lines': a furniture line of hand-made chairs upholstered in àdìrẹ and asò-oké, carrying Yoruba textile culture into contemporary design.

projects.title: Fourth Mainland Bridge Proposal
projects.blurb: Part of the six-person team behind the proposed double-decker bridge linking Ajah and Ikorodu — unbuilt, but a statement of infrastructural ambition for Lagos.

projects.title: Ilé Ilà at Homo Faber
projects.blurb: Her furniture exhibited at the Homo Faber craft biennial in Venice, placing Lagos workshop production in the European luxury-craft canon.
